A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Πnet research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original optimization benchmarks, motion-planning experiments, second-order-cone results, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds comparative second-order-cone results, sensitivity studies, and numerical validation of the backward pass.

M1.justification: The Douglas–Rachford projection algorithm, implicit backward pass using BiCGSTAB, training objective, matrix equilibration, and auto-tuning procedure remain unchanged. The expanded constraint list and differentiation discussion do not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic convex/nonconvex optimization, MPC, multi-vehicle and image-context planning, and second-order-cone programs. Revised SOC dimensions and additional diagnostics remain within this existing task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix B.5 expands from Πnet-only SOC results to comparisons against cvxpylayers and SCS, with SCS evaluated both directly and through CVXPY. This introduces substantive comparative evaluation for the SOC experiments; comparator membership in the retained benchmarks is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix B.5 changes SOC dimensions from (250,250) to (25,25) and (500,500), and batch size B from 1024 to 128, retaining 1000 epochs. New sensitivity experiments vary iteration counts and splitting parameters. Appendix F.3 introduces finite-difference gradient checks on two fixed instances with 200 forward iterations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained equilibration and auto-tuning ablations, v2 adds test-time iteration sweeps and sensitivity to sigma and omega (Figures 18–20). Appendix F.3 and Figure 22 newly test backward-pass accuracy against finite differences as the number of backward iterations varies.

E5.justification: v1 states that SOC experiments use 100 seeds. v2 removes that statement and reports means and standard deviations across five seeds for its revised SOC experiments in Figure 15. Seed counts and uncertainty summaries for retained benchmark plots remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v1's SOC result statement that RS and CV remain below 10^-6 is replaced by results under revised settings, including Figures 14–15 and Table 5. The new large-SOC batch timings are 0.90982 seconds for Πnet and 10.97265 for direct SCS. Sensitivity and VJP-accuracy results are also added; retained benchmark table values and plot data are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix F.1 adds an argument for almost-everywhere differentiability using the projection's 1-Lipschitz property and Rademacher's theorem. F.2 discusses conditional nonsmooth implicit differentiation while explicitly deferring a full analysis. Existing algorithm derivations, convergence arguments, and complexity analysis remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement strengthen the comparative claim to orders-of-magnitude advantages in training time, solution quality, and tuning robustness. The conclusion adds that Πnet succeeds where existing learning methods fail. The underlying method and application contributions remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds guidance about reducing test-time iterations and qualifications concerning nonsmooth differentiation and heuristic gradients. It also describes JAXopt as significantly worse rather than similar despite retaining Figure 2. New SOC interpretations include overstatements: Table 5 shows Πnet slower than direct SCS for a single large problem.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the native SCS and CVXPY parametric interfaces used in the added comparisons. Appendix F.3 documents Gaussian sampling scale, a finite-difference step of 10^-6, and forward-iteration settings. Existing hardware, code access, backbone, equilibration, and auto-tuning information is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning constrained sampling, neural MPC, homeomorphic projections, and conservative gradients/nonsmooth implicit differentiation. Some earlier references, including system-level synthesis and structured prediction, disappear. The central positioning as a specialized implicit projection layer remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The narrative largely survives with localized rewrites, an explicit constraint-type list, and condensed hyperparameter prose. Section 2.5 moves to Appendix C.5. v2 adds contents and figure/table lists and changes citations to author–year style, without broadly restructuring the argument.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with six new numbered figures covering SOC comparisons, sensitivity studies, and gradient accuracy, plus a new SOC timing table. Existing figures are mostly reused and relocated or renumbered, alongside conference-template, table-formatting, and page-layout changes.

improvement.justification: The new finite-difference validation directly tests the approximate backward pass, while expanded SOC comparisons and parameter sweeps strengthen empirical support. These gains are limited by reporting inaccuracies: Table 5 contradicts the claimed single-large-problem speed advantage over SCS, and Figure 14 does not support uniformly lower CV than cvxpylayers. The differentiation discussion also stops short of a complete justification.
